# A Brief History of Lighthouses

For as long as people have sailed, they have needed a way to find the shore in darkness. The earliest navigational lights were simple bonfires kept burning on hilltops and headlands, tended by communities whose livelihoods depended on ships returning safely. As maritime trade grew, these fires were raised onto platforms and then purpose-built towers to make them visible from farther out to sea.

The most celebrated ancient lighthouse was the Pharos of Alexandria, completed around 280 BCE under Ptolemy II. Rising more than 100 metres, it was among the tallest structures in the world and one of the Seven Wonders. A fire burned at its summit by night, and a mirror is said to have reflected sunlight by day. It stood for well over a thousand years before earthquakes brought it down, and its name survives in the word for lighthouse in several languages, including the French *phare* and Spanish *faro*. The Romans extended the practice across their empire, building towers at Ostia, Dover, and La Coruña, where the Tower of Hercules still operates today.

After Rome's decline, lighthouse construction slowed in Europe, with lights often maintained by monasteries or local authorities. The revival came with the expansion of commerce in the early modern period. The great engineering challenge was building on exposed, wave-swept rocks. The Eddystone Lighthouse off the coast of Plymouth illustrates the struggle: Henry Winstanley's first tower of 1698 was destroyed in the Great Storm of 1703, and its wooden successor burned. John Smeaton's 1759 version, built of interlocking granite blocks with hydraulic lime and shaped like an oak trunk, set the pattern for rock lighthouses for the next century.

Illumination improved alongside structure. Open coal fires and candles gave way to oil lamps, and in 1782 Aimé Argand's hollow-wick lamp produced a steadier, brighter flame. The decisive breakthrough came in 1822, when Augustin-Jean Fresnel devised a lens of concentric glass prisms that gathered scattered light into a single powerful beam. Fresnel lenses allowed a light to be seen more than twenty miles away and quickly became standard worldwide.

The nineteenth century was the golden age of lighthouse building, with thousands erected along the coasts of Europe, North America, and colonial shipping routes. Keepers and their families lived isolated lives, trimming wicks and winding clockwork mechanisms. Electricity and then automation gradually ended that way of life during the twentieth century.

Today, satellite navigation has reduced the practical importance of lighthouses, yet many remain active as backups, and others are preserved as museums and monuments to human ingenuity.
